# Self-Evaluation

## Purpose

Make every written artifact pass its own review before anyone else sees it.
The agent that produced the file reads it again as a reviewer would, with the
file on disk as the only evidence, asks whether it is right and what would
make it better, applies the changes that are plainly improvements, and records
the rest. Self-evaluation runs by default on everything the scaffold writes
(`rules/common/self-review.md`). It comes before human approval and never
stands in for it.

## Use When

- A command has just written or rewritten a structured artifact in the
  workspace: a bible entry, a scene, a page file, a reference plan, a prompt
  package, a review file, a continuity state, an edition.
- `/self-review` runs on existing artifacts.
- A phase gate is about to be requested and the work should arrive clean.

## Inputs

- The artifact, read fresh from disk. Memory of writing it does not count.
- Its schema in `schemas/`, the rule layers that governed it (common, the
  relevant domain layers, and the one format layer the project uses), and
  the Quality Bar section of the skill that produced it.
- The upstream canon it derives from: the story bible, the character and
  location files, the scene, the page plan.

## Process

1. Read the artifact cold, in its on-disk form. What the author meant to
   write is no evidence of what the file says.
2. Schema gate. Run
   `node scripts/validate-workspace.js --root <workspace> --issue <ISS_ID>`
   and, for page files, also
   `node scripts/check-continuity.js --root <workspace> --issue <ISS_ID>`.
   Check IDs against the naming scheme and confirm that every
   cross-reference resolves: characters, props, wardrobe IDs, levels,
   landmarks, asset IDs, neighboring pages. A failure at this gate is fixed
   at once. No judgment is involved.
3. Rules gate. Check the artifact against each rule layer that governed it
   and cite the specific rule for anything it breaks. A page file answers to
   `rules/layout/` and `rules/lettering/`, a reference plan to
   `rules/image/reference-roles.md`, human-facing prose to
   `rules/writing/prose-style.md`.
4. Quality-bar gate. Go through the producing skill's Quality Bar point by
   point. A point passes when the file demonstrably meets it. "Nothing
   looks wrong" is not a pass.
5. Improvement pass. Name at least two concrete changes that would make the
   artifact better, then judge each one: does it serve the story and the
   canon, or is it churn? Apply the clear wins. Drop rewording that changes
   no decision, reference, or number.
6. Give one of three verdicts. `pass`: nothing found. `fixed`: findings were
   applied, with a list of what changed and why. `flagged`: a finding needs
   a human or an upstream decision. Record a flagged finding where the next
   person will see it (the artifact's `notes`, the story bible's
   `open_questions`, or `open_issues` in the continuity state) and name the
   decision needed.
7. Run the gates once more after any fix. Allow two repair cycles at most.
   If the artifact still fails, the defect is upstream, in a bible, a plan,
   or the brief, and the work goes there next
   (`rules/common/source-of-truth.md`).
8. Deliver the verdict with the work, in three lines or fewer: the verdict,
   the changes or the open decision, and which commands were run.

Rendered pages are outside this procedure. Whether a drawing shows the right
person in the right place is decided by `pixel-review`, which opens the image
and records evidence. Self-evaluation may check a review file for
completeness (every check has evidence, every `fixed` finding has a recheck),
but it never certifies the art, and a clean schema run says nothing about
identity, anatomy, or geography.

## Outputs

- The artifact, unchanged or improved in place, still valid against its
  schema.
- A short verdict delivered with the work: `pass`, `fixed` with the change
  list, or `flagged` with the decision needed and where it was recorded.

## Quality Bar

- Every verdict cites specific checks: a script result, a rule file, a
  quality-bar point. Overall impressions do not appear.
- Applied fixes preserve canon. Nothing established upstream is altered
  downstream without a record.
- Every flagged finding states the exact decision needed and who owns it.
- The improvement pass produced real candidates. "Nothing to improve" on a
  first draft is a warning sign.
- The verdict never describes a rendered page as checked, and never uses the
  word approved.
- No artifact went through more than two repair cycles here.

## Common Failure Modes

- Rubber-stamping: reading your own output with the author's eyes and
  finding it flawless. Score against the written quality bar.
- Polishing past the second cycle while the real defect sits upstream.
- Cosmetic churn counted as improvement.
- Patching a page file when the character file is wrong. The fix belongs
  upstream, and a downstream patch starts canon drift.
- Treating a self-review `pass` as approval. `draft`, `review`, `approved`
  still needs the human act (`rules/common/approval-policy.md`).
- Reporting a clean validation run as proof that the pages look right.
- Skipping the scripts and "validating" by reading the YAML.

## Notes

Self-evaluation is the producing agent's job at write time. `production-qa`
audits at phase gates and stays read-only. An artifact that skipped its
self-review and gets caught at a gate goes back to its owner with both
reports.

The three verdict words are shared with visual reviews, and the acts differ.
Here a verdict describes a structured file checked against rules. In a
`visual-review` file it describes pixels checked against the plan. Say which
one you mean when reporting.
